'''Robert M. Schofield''' (born 1960) is an American physicist and a research associate professor at the [[University of Oregon]] (UO). He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]  in 2014.

== Early life and education ==
Born in 1960,<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 11, 2022 |title=U.S., Index to Public Records, 1994-2019 |url=https://www.ancestry.com/discoveryui-content/view/81740034:62209 |url-access=subscription |website=www.ancestry.com}}</ref> Schofield holds bachelor's degrees in experimental psychology (1982) and in physics (1983) from [[Brigham Young University]]. He earned a Ph.D. in 1990 at the University of Oregon, with the dissertation, ''X-ray microanalytic concentration measurements in unsectioned specimens: A technique and its application to zinc, manganese, and iron enriched mechanical structures of organisms from three phyla'', advised by Harlan W. Lefevre.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last1=Schofield |first1=Robert M. S. |date=1990 |title=X-Ray Microanalytic Concentration Measurements in Unsectioned Specimens: a Technique and its Application to Zinc, Manganese, and Iron Enriched Mechanical Structures of Organisms from Three Phyla |url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/4e62763f267389dda9fcf6ea9ebf3d2f/1 |bibcode=1990PhDT.......283S |s2cid=135472065 }}</ref>

Schofield held postdoctoral positions in the university's Institute of Molecular Biology and at [[Lund University]]. He then joined the UO as a research faculty member,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2014-12-16 |title=Two UO scientists named fellows of American Physical Society |url=https://around.uoregon.edu/content/two-uo-scientists-named-fellows-american-physical-society |access-date=2022-09-07 |website=Around the O |language=en}}</ref> and was promoted in 2020 to research associate professor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2020 Faculty Promotions {{!}} Office of the Provost |url=https://provost.uoregon.edu/2020-faculty-promotions |access-date=2022-09-17 |website=provost.uoregon.edu}}</ref>

== Career ==
Schofield's research interests include [[Gravitational-wave astronomy|gravitational waves]] and structural [[biophysics]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Research Staff {{!}} Profile Categories {{!}} Department of Physics |url=https://physics.uoregon.edu/profiles/postdocs/#S |access-date=2022-09-08 |website=physics.uoregon.edu}}</ref> He has been described as "an inter-disciplinarian, merging principles from physics, biology and materials science in pursuit of his passions".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robert Schofield's research in The Conversation {{!}} Institute for Fundamental Science |url=https://ifs.uoregon.edu/2021/09/01/robert-schofield-in-the-conversation/ |access-date=2022-09-08 |website=ifs.uoregon.edu |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== LIGO ===
{{Quotebox
| text = Schofield also found an unusual noise source that was recurring on hot summer afternoons: ravens were pecking the ice on pipes from a nitrogen [[cryopump]] maintaining the vacuum inside LIGO's concrete arms. Schofield said, "They peck for a while and make themselves a snow cone."<ref name=":1" /> The remedy was to insulate the pipes to avoid attracting the ravens, and also to fix an instrument that jiggled when the ravens pecked.<ref name=":1" />
| author = 
| align = right
| width = 30%
| border = 1px
}}

Schofield's work to enhance the sensitivity of the [[LIGO|Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO)]] has allowed physicists to detect [[gravitational wave]]s produced by colliding black holes.<ref name=":0" /> LIGO's biggest challenge is detector noise,  from [[seismic wave]]s, [[Kinetic theory of gases|thermal motion]], and [[Phonon noise|photon shot noise]], disturbances that could mask signals from gravitational waves.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last=Berti |first=Emanuele |title=The First Sounds of Merging Black Holes |journal=Physics |year=2016 |volume=9|page=17 |doi=10.1103/Physics.9.17 |arxiv=1602.04476 |bibcode=2016PhyOJ...9...17B |s2cid=54655094 |doi-access=free }}</ref> LIGO can detect "a truck rumbling past, the humming of a refrigerator in a nearby building, or the distant flutter of a plane's propellers".<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Doughton |first=Sandi |date=2018-05-14 |title=Ripples in space-time or 3-pound bird? Ravens at Hanford foul test of Einstein's theory |language=en-US |website=[[The Seattle Times]] |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/science/suddenly-there-came-a-tapping-ravens-cause-blips-in-massive-physics-instrument-at-hanford/ |access-date=2022-09-17}}</ref>

Laura Hamers wrote, "Gravitational waves are so faint by the time they reach Earth that they can be drowned out by closer-to-home disturbances most of us wouldn't even notice. For example, the early LIGO detectors were so sensitive that water going over a dam 30 kilometers away could throw off the data, said Schofield, who co-leads the environmental monitoring at the Hanford detector. He and his colleagues have placed a bevy of sensors around the detectors, which keep track of external disruptions like rumbling traffic or crackling lightning."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-12-01 |title=New research effort shines more light on black hole collisions |url=https://around.uoregon.edu/content/new-research-effort-shines-more-light-black-hole-collisions |access-date=2022-09-17 |website=Around the O |language=en}}</ref>

Elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society, Schofield was cited for "leadership in identifying and mitigating environmental factors which impact the sensitivity of terrestrial gravitational wave detectors and elimination [of] spurious noise sources in LIGO."<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm |access-date=2022-09-07 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref>

=== Biophysics ===
[[BBC News]] said of Schofield's findings, "Central American leaf-cutter ants 'retire' from their cutting role when they grow old, switching to carrying when their jaws blunt with age... Dr Schofield and his team used electron microscopy to compare the pristine teeth of laboratory-reared pupae with the worn teeth of the wild forager ants."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Brennard |first=Ema |date=2011-01-07 |title=Leaf-cutter ants' teeth wear out |language=en-GB |work=British Broadcasting Corporation |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/earth/hi/earth_news/newsid_9306000/9306830.stm |access-date=2022-11-18}}</ref>

Schofield has found similarities between his research methods in biology and physics. For example, [[micromanipulator]]s used in physics to guide a laser beam can be reconfigured to move an ant mandible through a leaf, allowing measurement of force. In addition, calculations Schofield uses in biology are similar to calculations in his work at LIGO.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cooper |first=Matt |date=2013-07-09 |title=Physicist finds new world with leaf-cutter ants |url=https://around.uoregon.edu/content/physicist-finds-new-world-leaf-cutter-ants |access-date=2022-11-18 |website=Around the O |language=en}}</ref>

In January 2016, Schofield and five undergraduate researchers published a paper in [[Royal Society Open Science]], making video clips of ants' leaf processing behaviors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Garrett |first1=Ryan W. |last2=Carlson |first2=Katherine A. |last3=Goggans |first3=Matthew Scott |last4=Nesson |first4=Michael H. |last5=Shepard |first5=Christopher A. |last6=Schofield |first6=Robert M. S. |title=Leaf processing behaviour in Atta leafcutter ants: 90% of leaf cutting takes place inside the nest, and ants select pieces that require less cutting |journal=Royal Society Open Science |year=2016 |volume=3 |issue=1 |article-number=150111 |doi=10.1098/rsos.150111  |doi-access=free|pmc=4736916 |pmid=26909161|bibcode=2016RSOS....350111G }}</ref> They "documented never-before-seen looks at the ants' prehensile skills — they're good at grabbing — and the layers of behaviors associated with gathering leaves, delivering them to the nests and processing them to grow the fungus that colony members eat".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-28 |title=Skilled workers: Study shows the talents of leafcutter ants |url=https://around.uoregon.edu/content/skilled-workers-study-shows-talents-leafcutter-ants |access-date=2022-09-08 |website=Around the O |language=en}}</ref>

Schofield and 15 students from University of Oregon and [[Lane Community College]] conducted studies in 2021 that led to the discovery of the heavy element materials zinc and manganese in "ant mandibles, spider fangs and scorpion sting tips" that harden and sharpen their cutting tools.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barlow |first=Jim |date=2021-09-02 |title=Special materials boost the bite power of small critters |url=https://around.uoregon.edu/content/special-materials-boost-bite-power-small-critters |access-date=2022-09-18 |website=Around the O |language=en}}</ref>

=== Mentoring ===
Schofield served as a mentor for McNair Scholars at UO between 2015 and 2017, supervising student participation in biology and biochemistry projects.<ref>{{Cite web |title=McNair Scholars {{!}} Undergraduate Research and Distinguished Scholarships |url=https://urds.uoregon.edu/awards/mcnair |access-date=2022-11-18 |website=urds.uoregon.edu}}</ref>
